what_its_for: Rituximab-pvvr is a medicine used to treat certain types of cancer (such as non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia) and some autoimmune diseases (such as rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and microscopic polyangiitis). It works by targeting and destroying certain white blood cells called B-cells that are causing harm in your body.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly dripped into your vein through a needle or catheter. A healthcare provider will give it to you in a clinic or hospital setting. You will NOT give this medication to yourself at home. Each infusion may take several hours, so plan to spend a significant amount of time at your appointment. You may be given other medications before your infusion (such as antihistamines, fever reducers, and steroids) to help reduce the chance of a reaction.
dosing: Your dose and how often you receive it depends on the condition being treated and your body size (weight). Common schedules include once a week for 4 doses, or once every few weeks as part of a chemotherapy plan. Your doctor will decide the exact dose and schedule that is right for you. Never try to adjust your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare provider in a clinic, you will have a scheduled appointment for each dose. If you need to miss or reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or clinic as soon as possible. Try not to skip doses, as this can make your treatment less effective. Your care team will help you get back on track.
storage: You do not need to store this medication at home. The clinic or pharmacy prepares and stores it properly. If for any reason you are given information about storing it, keep it refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C), do not freeze it, and keep it away from light. Do not shake the medication.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick with colds, flu, or infections, as your immune system will be weakened. Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as the nasal flu spray, shingles vaccine Zostavax, or chickenpox vaccine) during treatment and for some time after, without talking to your doctor first. Avoid crowded places when possible. Tell all of your doctors and dentists that you are receiving this medication before any procedures. Avoid becoming pregnant during treatment.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you experience: trouble breathing, chest pain, or a feeling that your heart is racing during or after your infusion; signs of a serious infection such as fever over 100.4°F (38°C), chills, or painful urination; unusual sores in your mouth or throat; severe skin reactions like blistering, peeling, or a rash; sudden numbness, weakness, confusion, or vision problems (which could be signs of a rare but serious brain infection called PML); yellowing of your skin or eyes; or any new or worsening symptoms. Also call your doctor if you feel an infusion reaction such as dizziness, hives, swelling, or shortness of breath during treatment.
when_it_works: How quickly you notice results depends on what condition is being treated. For some cancers, it may take several weeks to months to see a full response. For autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, you may begin to notice improvement within a few weeks to a few months after starting treatment. Your doctor will monitor your progress with blood tests and check-ups throughout your treatment.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not use this medication if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 12 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose. Older adults: Older patients may have a higher risk of certain side effects, including heart and lung problems, so your doctor will monitor you closely. Children: Safety and dosing in children depends on the specific condition being treated; your child's doctor will guide you. Kidney or liver problems: Make sure your doctor knows if you have any kidney or liver issues, as this may affect your treatment plan.
